newsitem.title: USA: International Paper to sell assets, cut 9,000 jobs.
newsitem.headline: International Paper to sell assets, cut 9,000 jobs.

text.p: International Paper Co. on Tuesday unveiled plans to sell $1 billion worth of assets over the next year and chop 9,000 jobs -- about 10 percent of its work force -- in an effort to improve its sagging financial performance.
"We will be divesting or closing operations that no longer meet the company's financial or strategic objectives," International Paper Chairman John Dillon said in a statement announcing the moves.
Wall Street analysts hailed the steps as long overdue.

The paper and forestry products company will shut down three production lines at its Erie, Pa., mill and will close its mill in Woronoco, Mass., it said. It also will close its de-inking pulp operation in Lock Haven, Pa.

While International Paper plans to shed 9,000 workers, fewer than half of the cuts will come as layoffs, company spokesman Phillip Giaramita said. For instance, nearly 4,800 jobs will be transferred with the planned sale of its imaging and multi-wall kraft -- or strong brown paper -- businesses, he said.
Planned asset sales also include International Paper's packaging businesses and 175,000 acres of timberland in western regions of Pennsylvania and New York, the company said.

Giaramita said the assets identified for sale Tuesday do not make up all of the $1 billion worth the company expects to sell this year. Other businesses will be sold as the company continues its review of operations.
International Paper also said it would convert production lines in Maine and Alabama, cutting its pulp and uncoated paper capacity by at least 400,000 tons.

The company had become too diversified, and for some time has needed to get rid of operations that have contributed to its recent reputation as a sluggish performer, Smith Barney analyst Josh Kapp said.
"They had diversified into businesses that haven't been successful," Kapp said.
In a conference call with analysts, company officials said they will apply most of gain from the asset sales to cutting International Paper's $9.905 billion debt load.
The company also expects to realise about $100 million in savings from the job cuts and plant closings and another $80 million in savings from reduced interest from debt, analysts said.
The restructuring will begin contributing to earnings this year and will have a greater impact in 1998, when most of the actions are completed, the company said.
It said the moves will not affect its $1.2 billion capital spending plans for 1998.

The restructuring will cost International Paper $535 million in pretax charges in the second quarter, the company said. It is also recording a separate charge of $150 million to add to its legal reserve.

In preliminary earnings released Tuesday, the company said the charges will force it to post a loss for the second quarter of about $419 million, or $1.39 per share, vs. a profit of $99 million, or 33 cents per share, a year ago.
Despite the loss, the company said demand remains strong, and it had a second-quarter operating profit of 20 cents per share before the restructuring charges.
It recorded sales for the quarter of $5.034 billion, down slightly from $5.093 billion a year ago.
"The good demand we are experiencing should lead to increased profitability over the next six months," Dillon said.
The company's stock jumped on the news, closing $4.69 higher at $56 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"This is great," said Bear, Stearns analyst Linda Lieberman. " They're finally starting to do what they need to do. It's something they've been needing to do for a long while."
